A Republican strategy to block Obama's re-election
The Republican leaders justified their policy by the need to fight against electoral fraud.
Now, the Brennan Center considers this last point a myth and claims that election fraud is less common in the United States than the number of people who die from lightning strikes.
In fact, Republican lawyers have found only 300 cases of election fraud in the United States in ten years.
One thing is certain: those new provisions will negatively affect the voter turnout rate.
In that sense, these measures will undermine part of the American democratic system.
Unlike the situation in Canada, the states of the United States are responsible for organizing federal elections.
And along those lines, a majority of American governments enacted, starting in 2009, new laws that made it harder to register or vote.
This phenomenon has spread after the November 2010 elections, which saw the addition of 675 new Republican representatives in 26 states.
As a result, during the year 2011, 180 bills restricting the right to vote were introduced in 41 states.
The new election laws require voters to present an ID with a photograph, as well as proof of American citizenship.

On the other hand, those laws reduce the periods for early voting, invalidate the right to register as a voter on the day of the election and remove the right to vote from citizens with criminal records.
Before the 2006 elections, no American state required voters to present an ID with a photograph.
The State of Indiana was the first to require it.
The U.S. Supreme Court confirmed in 2008 the constitutionality of the Indiana law.
Therefore, the Republican authorities hastened to extend that practice to other states.
In recent years these authorities have supported bills in 34 states to force voters to present an ID with a photograph.
It is important to note that, unlike the situation in Quebec, American citizens do not have a universal identification document, such as the Social Security card.
In fact, 11% of American citizens, that is, 21 million voters, do not have any government-issued photo ID.
On the other hand, five million new voters in 2012 lack an ID with those characteristics.
But often, the cost of obtaining the required identification document exceeds one hundred dollars.
As a result, the new restrictions disproportionately affect young people, minorities, and low-income individuals.
Indeed, 25% of African Americans, 15% of people earning less than $35,000 a year, 18% of citizens over 65, and 20% of voters aged 18 to 29 do not have a photo ID.
And there's more.
In many states, students, the voters who most vote for Democratic candidates, cannot use the photo ID card issued by their institution.
On the other hand, those same states allow members of hunting and fishing clubs to use the documents issued by those clubs.
Before 2004, no state required a citizenship test to vote.
Arizona was the first state to make such a demand.
Since 2011, a dozen states have enacted laws requiring voters to show they are American citizens.
Those measures clearly aim to limit the vote of Hispanics.
It seems that two out of every three Hispanic voters support the Democratic Party.
On the other hand, Republican legislators supported in 2011 certain laws that abolished same-day voter registration in eight states.
In addition, they limited the right of individuals and groups to provide assistance to voters who wanted to register.
These restrictions have consequences.
For example, in the 2004 general elections, voter registration campaigns contributed to the registration of about 10 million citizens.
The measures taken since 2009 caused the registration rate of new voters to fall in 2010 compared to 2006.
In addition, Republican legislators passed laws in five other states that favored early voting.
For example, in the 2008 elections in Florida, 33% of the voters who voted early were African American, while these voters represented only 13% of the electorate in the state.
In the case of the Spanish, the same thing happened.
These represent no more than 11% of the voters, which is equivalent to 24% of the citizens who vote in advance.
However, the whites, who represent 76% of the electorate, represent only 46% of the voters who vote in advance.
Of course, the democratic legislators and their supporters have strongly opposed the adoption of laws that restrict voter registration.
In this regard, democratic governors have blocked several bills.
The U.S. Attorney General's Office intervened to suspend the most controversial laws.
The damage could be, in part, limited.
For example, only 16 of 34 states adopted the law requiring the presentation of an ID with a photo.
However, it is undeniable that the new rules adopted will complicate the exercise of the right to vote in 2012.
Critics from the Democratic Party are denouncing the partisan nature of the laws that have been passed, as it is clear that with them they intend to influence the results of 2012 in the key states.
A 2011 Brennan Center report shows that states that have adopted such laws represent 171 of the 270 votes needed in the electoral college to win the presidency.
It is too early to say with certainty whether these legislative changes at the level of the electoral system will have a significant impact on the results of the 2012 presidential elections.
One thing is certain: those new provisions will negatively affect the voter turnout rate.
In this regard, the measures will undermine part of the American democratic system.

On the other hand, many desire fervently that they meet, since the smallest difference could open a door to a "new physics" that would plug certain holes in the model.

But we have not found such differences at CERN so far.

They glimpsed the scientific applications, but nothing more.

For example, the same Willard Boyle developed a light detector in 1969 during his research on optics.
Although it was not his original intention at all, this detector now serves as an "eye" for all the world's digital devices, which earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009.
That doesn't mean, of course, that the activities of the LHC necessarily want to transform our lives, but we never know...

In its Commission on Dignified Death, Quebec recently debated the delicate issue of end-of-life.
The debate should be resumed soon while preparing a bill.
Now, within that essential domain, there is still a lot to do.
The Devoir has tried to get close to him.
Just a few weeks ago, Mr. L. lived alone in his apartment in Montérégie.
The prostate cancer that was destroying him had given him two years of relief.
"They gave me five years of life, but I've already been here seven," he says, lying in bed at the Victor-Gadbois Palliative Care Centre in Beloeil, where he arrived the day before.
"But it's always a shock, we can't be prepared for this," he continues.
The illness has caused him great weakness: he cannot go to the bathroom alone or even eat by himself.
Sitting in front of a tempting lunch, he accepts resignedly that he will be helped to eat.
Brave, he even smiles, talks to strangers who pay attention to him, bring him medicine, and offer him a bath.
The courage of ordinary death.
"My greatest wish is that they cure my diarrhea, it's humiliating," he confesses.
A few hours later, the team found a cure for that illness.
"During our lives we learn that a man urinates standing up," says Pierre Brodeur, a psychologist at the Victor-Gadbois Center.
Returning to one's childhood, for certain people, is an unacceptable humiliation.
"That depends on the person's ability to accept that regression," he notes.
Because, according to the opinion of most people who work in palliative care, the big moments take place in the very heart of that regression.
All patients who enter the Victor-Gadbois Palliative Care Centre suffer from cancer.
They have a maximum life expectancy of three months.
In that state, the team of doctors and nurses who surround them no longer offer "curative" care.
The greatest fear of Mrs. A., 89, is to die "conscious and drowned."
But the illness has made him discover his children.
"I have some good children," he adds.
"I have no more wishes in this life," she says, before accepting that a mask be placed on her to help her breathe.
And wait, in the next days, a last visit from his son who lives in Italy.
In Victor-Gadbois, with a group of volunteers, the care of the body and help with feeding is offered.
These are comfort measures that are given when there's nothing else that can be done.
To help make his death more comfortable.
In Quebec, we have one palliative care bed for every 11,700 residents.
It's very little, since we know that we will all die one day.
Here, life continues under the best possible conditions, explains Dr. Christiane Martel, one of the doctors at the center.
Whether at the level of physical comfort, emotional or spiritual.
The dying man is offered mouth washes with brandy or Pepsi, according to demand.
Diabetics are no longer monitored for their blood sugar levels.
Death is part of everyday life.
Last night we served Mr. X a beer, who died during the night.
This morning, his son finished the beer at the feet of the deceased.
"We help both the patients and their loved ones," says Nathalie Savard, director of care.
In the center Victor-Gadbois, the days pass without ever being the same.

While a 94-year-old man savors his last family gathering in the yard, comfortably seated on his pillows while everyone toasts to his health, a 36-year-old man tragically dies surrounded by his parents, his wife, and his two children, after having tried everything to survive.
"For the past six months, there have been three to five occupied beds for people under 45 with cancer," worries Dr. Christiane Martel.

A 77% of Canadians simply have no access to palliative care, that is, to care designed to relieve suffering when a patient reaches the terminal phase of his life, whether at home, in a hospital or in a care center.

"Recently," he says, "I have seen a patient spend 14 days in the emergency room suffering from great pain without the necessary measures being taken to relieve her."
I fear that patients will want to die because they are not receiving adequate care.
And in parallel, many oncologists persist with their patients until the last day, despite the worst prognoses.

It was possible, in part, to limit the damage.
For example, only 16 of the 34 states adopted the law requiring the presentation of an identity document with a photograph.
However, it is undeniable that the new rules adopted will complicate the exercise of the right to vote in 2012.
Critics from the Democratic Party are denouncing the partisan nature of the laws that have been voted, since it is clear that with them they want to influence the results of 2012 in the key states.
A 2011 Brennan Center report shows that states that have adopted such laws represent 171 of the 270 electoral votes needed to win the presidency.
It is too early to say with certainty whether these legislative changes at the electoral system level will have a significant impact on the results of the 2012 presidential elections.
One thing is certain: these new provisions will negatively affect the participation rate.
In this regard, the measures will undermine part of the American democratic system.
Prostate Cancer Detection: To get tested or not to get tested?
Indeed, the PSA test sometimes produces erroneous results, with false negatives or even false positives, leading to unnecessary medical interventions.
It's a sufficient reason for men, already reluctant by nature, to doubt whether they should undergo the tests.
To take the test or not?
We have consulted two experts.
In studies conducted in the United States, a high rate of infection was detected among the sample groups, making it difficult to interpret those data and make firm recommendations.
On the other hand, the European study showed some difference in mortality between patients who had undergone detection and those who had not.
The study, with a follow-up at 12 years, also showed that there is a 30 to 40% chance of developing metastases if the test is not done.
I recommend, therefore, the test from the age of 50, or from the age of 40 if your father has had prostate cancer.
African-American men have a higher risk index.
The key is to make a good decision once cancer is detected.
There are aggressive cancers and other cancers that are indolent.

It is truly necessary to ensure that the patient understands the risk level of his cancer. All possible options should be offered to him, and not necessarily treat prostate cancers that do not threaten long-term life, in which case active monitoring of the disease is preferable.
Today, many men who have been diagnosed with cancer are not treated, because the cancer is not aggressive and does not pose a risk to their lives.
Instead, we suggest active monitoring of the disease and, if it progresses, we offer treatment.
We are increasingly determining precise criteria to decide who should or should not be treated.
I recommend that the test be done in any case.
But it is important that you speak with your doctor to determine whether or not you should take the test.
Movember, in collaboration with the International Society of Urology, has created a tool that allows the evaluation of the pros and cons of the PSA test.
You can download this document (for now only in English, but translations will be available shortly) from the following link: http://ca.movember.com/fr/mens-health/prostate-cancer-screening
Prevent the disease
Unfortunately, there is no miracle cure for cancer.
Despite the progress in research, adopting healthy lifestyle habits remain the best way to reduce the risk of suffering from the disease.
We estimate that if everyone ate well and moved enough, 30% of cancers could be prevented.
"If no one smoked, that rate would be at least 50%", emphasizes André Beaulieu, spokesperson for the Canadian Cancer Society.
On the other hand, we estimate that about 10% of cancers are hereditary.
Many others remain completely inexplicable.
For the Canadian Cancer Society, the fight against smoking remains a priority despite the decrease in the number of smokers.
Tobacco is linked to 85% of lung cancer cases.
It also constitutes a risk factor for other types of cancer.
It seriously harms people's health.
"Today, there are still 1.5 million smokers in Quebec," said spokesperson André Beaulieu.
A hopeful fact: ten years after quitting smoking, the risk of dying from cancer is halved.
The peso
According to the SCC, fatness and obesity also favor the appearance of the disease.
The risks of breast, colon and rectal, esophageal, pancreatic and uterine cancer increase.
"Studies show that regular physical activity throughout life protects against breast cancer," they add.
The food
The organization also recommends limiting the consumption of red meat.
In large amounts, they increase the risk of developing colorectal cancer.
Meat products should also be avoided.
The preservation of meat for smoking, drying, or salting may cause the formation of carcinogenic substances.
"They can damage the cells of the organism and lead to the development of cancer," they explain to us.
The vitamins
In recent years, several scientists have studied the links between the vitamin complexes and cancer.
However, at the moment their investigations are not conclusive.
According to the SCC, studies about vitamin E are contradictory.
While in one of them a decrease in the risk of prostate cancer was observed, in the other, what was observed was rather an increase.
The effect of vitamin D on cancer has not been clearly determined.
On the other hand, M. Beaulieu insists on the importance of discussing one's concerns and family history with their doctor.
"Taking the test does not cause cancer."

The announcement of the probable discovery of the Higgs boson caused great commotion last summer, and rightly so.
It is indeed believed that this boson is part of the mechanism responsible for the mass of everything that exists in the universe, nothing more and nothing less.

And what's more, it's the particle whose existence was predicted by the standard model: our best or "least bad" explanation of nature and the behavior of matter, which has not yet been observed empirically.
But for physicists, it is not entirely clear whether it is the Higgs.
We are certain that a new particle exists and that it resembles the Higgs boson predicted by the standard model.
In addition, new data revealed this week at an important physics congress held in Kyoto seem to confirm that it is, although more data are still needed to be completely sure.

Palliative care. The best way to die... | The Devoir
In its "Dignity in Death" committee, Quebec recently debated the delicate issue of end-of-life.
The debate should be resumed soon as the bill is prepared.
Now, within that essential domain, there is still much to be done.
Le Devoir has tried to get close to him.
Just a few weeks ago, Mr. L. was living alone in his apartment in Montérégie.
The prostate cancer that was destroying him had given him two years of relief.
"They gave me five years of life, but I've already had seven," he says, lying on his bed in the Victor-Gadbois palliative care center in Beloeil, where he arrived the day before.
"But it's always a shock, we can't be prepared for this," he continues.
The illness has caused him great weakness: he is unable to go to the bathroom alone or even to eat by himself.
Sitting in front of a tempting lunch, he reluctantly accepts help to eat.
Brave, he even smiles, talks to strangers who pay attention to him, bring him medicine, and offer him a bath.
The courage of ordinary death.
"My greatest wish is that they cure my diarrhea, it's humiliating," he confesses.
A few hours later, the team found a cure for that illness.
"Throughout our lives we learn that a man urinates standing up," says Pierre Brodeur, a psychologist at the Victor-Gadbois Centre.
For some people, returning to childhood is an unacceptable humiliation.
"That depends on the person's ability to accept that regression," he states.
Because, according to the opinion of most people who work in palliative care, the big moments take place in the very heart of that regression.
All patients who enter the Victor-Gadbois Palliative Care Centre suffer from cancer.
They have a maximum life expectancy of three months.
In that state, the team of doctors and nurses who surround them no longer offer the "curative" care.
The greatest fear of Mrs. A., 89, is to die "conscious and drowned".
But the illness has made him reveal to his children.
"I have some good children," he adds.
"I have no more wishes in this life," she says before accepting that a mask be placed on her to help her breathe.
And wait, in the coming days, a final visit from his son who lives in Italy.
In Victor-Gadbois, with a group of volunteers, care of the body and help with feeding is offered.
These are the palliative care that is given when nothing else can be done.
To help make his death more comfortable.
In Quebec, we have a palliative care bed for every 11,700 residents.
It's very little, since we know that we will all die one day.
Here, life continues under the best possible conditions, explains Dr. Christiane Martel, one of the doctors at the center.
Whether on the level of physical comfort, emotional or spiritual.
The dying man is offered mouthwashes with brandy or Pepsi, according to demand.
Diabetics are no longer monitored for their blood sugar levels.
Death is part of everyday life.
Last night we served beer to Mr. X, who died during the night.
This morning, his son finished the beer at the feet of the deceased.
"We help both the patients and their loved ones," says Nathalie Savard, director of care.
At the Victor-Gadbois Centre, days pass without ever being the same.

Next to a 94-year-old man who is savoring his last family gathering in the yard, comfortably seated between his pillows while everyone drinks to his health, a 36-year-old man tragically dies, surrounded by his parents, his wife, and his two children, after having tried everything to survive
"For the past six months, there have always been three to five occupied beds for people under 45 with cancer," worries Dr. Christiane Martel.
53% of the patients admitted to the Victor-Gadboisarrivent center come from their home and 47% from the hospital.
Access to palliative care problem

A 77% of Canadians simply have no access to palliative care, that is, to care designed to relieve suffering when a patient reaches the terminal phase of his life, whether at home, in a hospital or in a care center.
And several organizations, such as the Victor-Gadbois Centre and the Home Palliative Care Society of Grand Montréal, specialize almost exclusively in the care of cancer patients.
It is precisely that great relative lack of healthcare in Quebec that makes many doctors specializing in palliative care fear the adoption of a law regulating euthanasia and assisted suicide.

Since October, a manifesto signed by leading figures in palliative care, such as Dr. Balfour Mount and Dr. Bernard Lapointe, has been circulating to demonstrate their opposition to such an initiative.
According to Dr. Christiane Martel, the healthcare system in Quebec is not competent enough to ensure that anyone has the right to quality palliative care before proceeding with euthanasia.
"Recently," she says, "I've seen a patient spend 14 days in the Emergency Department suffering from great pain without the necessary measures being taken to relieve her."
I fear that patients may want to die because they are not receiving adequate care.
And in parallel, many oncologists persist with their patients until the last day, despite the worst prognoses.
Hélène Richard's hopes of survival were already at a low when she left an exhausting chemotherapy treatment.
"When I told my oncologist I wanted to stop treatment, she said she was very sorry I wanted to stop fighting," he says.

A Republican strategy to block Obama's re-election
Republican leaders justified their policy by the need to combat electoral fraud.
However, the Brennan Center considers this last point a myth and claims that election fraud is less common in the United States than the number of people who die from lightning strikes.
In fact, Republican lawyers have found no more than 300 cases of election fraud in the United States in ten years.
One thing is certain: these new provisions will negatively affect the voter turnout rate.
In that sense, these measures will undermine the American democratic system to some extent.
Unlike Canada, the American states are responsible for organizing federal elections in the United States.
And in that same vein, a majority of American governments enacted, starting in 2009, new laws that made it more difficult to register or vote.
This phenomenon has spread after the November 2010 elections, which saw the addition of 675 new Republican representatives in 26 states.
As a result, during the year 2011, 180 bills restricting the exercise of the right to vote in 41 states were introduced.
The new electoral laws require voters to present an ID document with a photograph, as well as proof of American citizenship.
On the other hand, these laws reduce the periods for early voting, invalidate the right to register as a voter on election day, and remove the right to vote from citizens with criminal records.
Before the 2006 elections, no American state required voters to present an ID with a photograph.
The State of Indiana was the first to demand it.
In 2008, the U.S. Supreme Court confirmed the constitutionality of the Indiana law.
Therefore, the Republican authorities hastened to extend that practice to other states.
In recent years, these authorities have supported legislation in 34 states to force voters to present a photo ID.
It is important to note that, unlike the situation in Quebec, American citizens do not have a universal identification document, such as the Social Security card.
In fact, 11% of American citizens, that is, 21 million people of voting age, do not have any government-issued photo ID from a state agency.
On the other hand, five million new voters in 2012 lack an ID document with those characteristics.
But, often, obtaining the required identification document costs more than a hundred dollars.
Thus, the new restrictions disproportionately affect young people, minorities, and people with low incomes.
Indeed, 25% of African Americans, 15% of people earning less than $35,000 a year, 18% of citizens over 65 years old, and 20% of voters aged 18 to 29 do not have a photo ID.
And there's more.
In many states, students, the voters who most vote for Democratic candidates, cannot use the photo ID card issued by their institution.
On the other hand, those same states authorize members of hunting or fishing clubs, who often vote Republican, to use documents issued by those clubs.
Before 2004, no state required a citizenship test to vote.
Arizona was the first state to make such a demand.
Since 2011, a dozen states have enacted laws requiring voters to demonstrate that they are American citizens.
Those measures clearly aim to limit Hispanic voting.
It seems that two out of every three Hispanic voters support the Democratic Party.
On the other hand, Republican legislators supported in 2011 certain laws that eliminated same-day voter registration in eight states.
In addition, they limited the right of individuals and groups to create a voter assistance service for those who wanted to register.
These restrictions have consequences.
For example, in the 2004 general elections, voter registration campaigns contributed to the registration of about 10 million citizens.
The measures taken since 2009 have resulted in a drop in the rate of new voter registration in 2010 compared to the year 2006.
In addition, Republican legislators enacted laws in five other states that favored the reduction of early voting periods.
For example, in the 2008 elections in Florida, 33% of the voters who voted early were African American, while these voters represented only 13% of the electorate in the state.
In the case of Hispanics, it was exactly the same.
These represent no more than 11% of the voters, which is equivalent to 24% of the citizens who vote by advance voting.
However, the whites, who represent 76% of the electorate, represent no more than 46% of the citizens who vote in advance.
Of course, Democratic legislators and their supporters have strongly opposed the adoption of laws that restrict voter registration.
In this regard, democratic governors have blocked several bills.
The U.S. Attorney General's Office intervened to suspend the most controversial laws.
The damage could, in part, be limited.
For example, only 16 of 34 states adopted the law requiring the presentation of an identity document with a photograph.
However, it is undeniable that the new rules adopted will complicate the exercise of the right to vote in 2012.
Democratic critics are denouncing the partisan nature of the laws that have been voted on, as it is clear that with them they intend to influence the results of 2012 in the key states.
A 2011 Brennan Center report shows that states that have adopted these laws account for 171 of the 270 electoral votes needed to win the presidency.
It is too early to say with certainty whether these legislative changes at the electoral system level will have a significant impact on the results of the 2012 presidential elections.
One thing is certain: these new provisions will negatively affect the voter turnout rate.
In this regard, the measures will undermine part of the American democratic system.
Prostate Cancer Detection: To get tested or not to get tested?
Indeed, the PSA test can, on occasion, produce erroneous results, with false negatives or even false positives, after which unnecessary medical interventions are performed.
It is more than sufficient reason for men, already reluctant by nature, to doubt whether they should or should not take the detection tests.
To get tested or not to get tested?
We have consulted two specialists.
Studies conducted in the United States detected a high rate of infection among sample groups, making it difficult to interpret those data and make firm recommendations.
On the other hand, the European study showed some difference in mortality between patients who had undergone screening and those who had not.
The study, with a 12-year follow-up, also showed that there is between a 30 and 40% chance of developing metastases if the test is not performed.
I therefore recommend the test from the age of 50, or from the age of 40 if your father has had prostate cancer.
Black men have a higher risk rate.
The key is to make a good decision once cancer is detected.
There are aggressive cancers and other cancers that are indolent.

It is truly necessary to ensure that the patient understands the degree of risk of his cancer. All possible options should be offered to him, and not necessarily treat prostate cancers that do not threaten long-term survival, in which case active surveillance of the disease should be chosen instead.
Today, many men who have been diagnosed with cancer are not treated, since the cancer is not aggressive and does not pose a risk to their lives.
Instead, we suggest active monitoring of the disease and, if it progresses, we offer treatment.
We are increasingly determining precise criteria to decide who should or should not be treated.
I recommend that the test be taken in any case.
But it's important that you talk to your doctor to determine whether you should get the test or not.
Movember, in collaboration with the International Society of Urology, has created a tool that allows evaluating the pros and cons of the PSA test.
You can download this document (for now only in English, but translations will be available shortly) at the following link: http://ca.movember.com/fr/mens-health/prostate-cancer-screening
Prevent the disease
Unfortunately, there is no miracle cure to prevent cancer.
Despite the progress in research, adopting healthy lifestyle habits remain the best way to reduce the risk of suffering from the disease.
We estimate that if everyone ate well and moved enough, 30% of cancers could be prevented.
"If no one smoked, that rate would rise by at least 50%," emphasizes André Beaulieu, spokesperson for the Canadian Cancer Society.
In contrast, we estimate that about 10% of cancers are hereditary.
Many others remain totally unexplained.
For the Canadian Cancer Society, the fight against smoking remains a priority despite the decline in the number of smokers.
Tobacco is linked to 85% of lung cancer cases.
It also constitutes a risk factor for other types of cancer.
It seriously harms people's health.
"Today, there are still 1.5 million smokers in Quebec," said spokesperson André Beaulieu.
A hopeful fact: 10 years after quitting smoking, the risk of dying from cancer is reduced by half.
The peso
Obesity and fatness also favor the appearance of the disease, according to the SCC.
They increase the risks of breast cancer, colon and rectal cancer, esophageal cancer, pancreatic cancer, and uterine cancer.
"Studies show that regular physical activity throughout life protects against breast cancer," they add.
The feeding
The body also recommends limiting the consumption of red meats.
In large amounts, they increase the risk of developing colorectal cancer.
Meat products should also be avoided.
The preservation of meat for smoking, drying, or salting may lead to the formation of carcinogenic substances.
"They can damage the body's cells and lead to the development of cancer," they explain.
The vitamins
In recent years, several scientists have studied the links between the complex vitamins and cancer.
However, at the moment their investigations are not conclusive.
According to the SCC, studies on vitamin E are contradictory.
While in one of them a decrease in the risk of prostate cancer was observed, in another, what was observed was, rather, an increase.
The effect of vitamin D on cancer has not been clearly determined.
On the other hand, M. Beaulieu insists on the importance of discussing one's concerns and family history with one's doctor.
"Taking the test does not cause cancer."
The Higgs boson in detail
The announcement of the probable discovery of the Higgs boson caused a great stir last summer, and rightly so.
Indeed, it is believed that this boson is part of the mechanism responsible for the mass of everything that exists in the universe, nothing more and nothing less.

And what's more, it's the particle whose existence predicted by the standard model: our best or "least bad" explanation of the nature and behavior of matter, which has not yet been observed empirically.
But for physicists, it is not entirely clear whether it is the Higgs.
We know for sure that there is a new particle and that it is very similar to the Higgs boson predicted by the standard model.
In addition, new data revealed this week at an important physics congress held in Kyoto seem to confirm that it is, although more data are still needed to be completely sure.
Anyway, we assume it's Higgs, since the chances of being wrong seem few. We'll see what it is.
There is, in this great world, a general and inescapable law that implies that two things cannot be in the same place at the same time.
There's no way to violate that rule, and don't try too hard, because you'll end up hurting yourself.

Physicists classify particles into two categories.
On one hand we have the good citizens called fermions, who obey wisely the Pauli principle.
And then there are the bosons, a dirty pack of anarchists who have no respect for anything, or at least not for this principle, which means they can be found in the same place and at the same time.

According to the website The Particle Adventure from the Berkeley Laboratories, which, by the way, is excellent, bosons are divided into two groups: mesons, about which we will not speak here, and the "force particles," through which the great forces of nature are propagated and with which the Higgs boson would
These bosons, it should be emphasized here, are not the exotic creatures that we might think.
In fact, if you manage to read this report, it's thanks to an extraordinarily banal boson: the photon, or the "light particle" that acts as the "messenger" of the electromagnetic force.
Indeed, when a particle with an electric charge accelerates or changes direction, it "messes up" the electromagnetic field in that immediate vicinity; a bit like when we throw a stone into a pond.
In this "disorder" arises an electromagnetic wave (of light, of infrared, of ultraviolet, etc.), and this wave is nothing else than a photon; that is, one of the bosons "carrying force".
More stable field
The same thing happens with the Higgs boson, with the difference that it is another field, the Higgs field, which needs to be "disordered" for this boson to appear.

Well, the Higgs field is much more stable than the electromagnetic field. To activate it, you need to reach extremely high energies, a bit like if it were a frozen pond, where only a heavy rock could slide across the surface.
Therefore, an enormous particle accelerator like the one at CERN (the Large Hadron Collider is a 27 km circumference ring!) is needed to reach such energy levels.
The analogy with the electromagnetic field is a new tool that explains the relationship between the Higgs and mass.
In fact, not all particles and not all materials interact with the electromagnetic field.
Some, like the imams, do, but others don't: a piece of paper, for example, will never remain stuck by itself to the door of a refrigerator.
And in the same way, not all particles interact with the Higgs field: those that do have mass, while the rest (like the photon, by the way) do not.
Well, what "can they contribute" to all those investigations?, asks Mrs. Plamondon.
For science, this serves to verify the validity of the Standard Model (SM), and allows physicists to scrutinize the differences between observations and the predictions of the SM.
On the other hand, many fervently desire that they be found, for the smallest difference could open a door to a "new physics" that would plug certain holes in the model.

This, one must say, still has enormous shortcomings, such as not proposing any explanation regarding gravity (¡ups!) or dark matter, which constitutes about 80% of the matter in the Universe (another ups!).
But we have not found such differences at CERN so far.
Repercussions

To show you: at the beginning of the 1960s, the pioneers of the laser in the laboratories did not at all suspect the revolution their work would provoke.
They foresaw scientific applications, but nothing more.

Imagine...
And in addition, the applications can also come from the entire instrumentation surrounding the research.
For example, the same Willard Boyle developed a light detector in 1969 during his research in the field of optics.
Although it was absolutely not his original intention, this detector now serves as an "eye" for all digital devices in the world, which earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2009.
That doesn't mean, of course, that LHC activities necessarily want to transform our lives, but we never know...
Palliative care. The best way to die... | Le Devoir
In its Commission on Dying with Dignity, Quebec recently debated the delicate issue of end-of-life.
The debate must be resumed soon as a bill is being prepared.
Now, within that essential domain, there is still much to do.
Le Devoir has tried to get close to it.
Just a few weeks ago, Mr. L. was living alone in his apartment in the Montérégie.
The prostate cancer that was destroying him had given him a two-year reprieve.

"I had been given five years of life, but I've already lived seven," he says, lying in bed at the Victor-Gadbois palliative care center in Beloeil, where he arrived the day before, his body a mass of pain.
"But it's always a shock, we can't be prepared for this," he continues.
The illness has taken a toll on him: a huge weakness that prevents him from going to the bathroom alone and even from eating by himself.
Sitting in front of an appetizing lunch, he accepts resignedly that they help him eat.
Brave, he even smiles, speaks to strangers who pay attention to him, bring him medicine, and offer him a bath.
The bravery of ordinary death.
"My greatest wish is that they cure my diarrhea, it's humiliating," he confesses.
A few hours later, the team found a remedy for that illness.
"Throughout our lives we learn that a man urinates standing up," says Pierre Brodeur, psychologist at the Victor-Gadbois centre.
For certain people, returning to their childhood is an unacceptable humiliation.
"That depends on the person's ability to accept that regression," he notes.
Because, according to the opinion of most people who work in palliative care, the big moments take place in the very heart of that regression.
All patients who enter the Victor-Gadbois Palliative Care Centre suffer from cancer.
They have a maximum life expectancy of three months.
In that state, the team of doctors and nurses who surround them no longer offer "curative" care.
The greatest fear of Mrs. A., who is 89 years old, is to die "conscious and drowned."
But the illness has made him discover his children.
"I have some good children," he adds.
"I have no more wishes in this life," she says, before accepting that a mask will be placed on her to help her breathe.
And he is expecting, in the coming days, a final visit from his son who lives in Italy.
In Victor-Gadbois, with a group of volunteers, care of the body and help with feeding is offered.
These are palliative care that are given when nothing else can be done.
To help make his death more comfortable.
In Quebec, we have a palliative care bed for every 11,700 residents.
It's very little, since we know that we will all eventually die one day.
Here, life continues in the best possible conditions, explains Dr. Christiane Martel, one of the center's doctors.
Whether at the level of physical comfort, emotional or spiritual.
Mouthwashes of brandy or Pepsi are offered to the dying, according to demand.
Diabetics are no longer monitored for their blood sugar levels.
Death is part of the everyday.
Last night we served a beer to Mr. X, who died during the night.
This morning, his son finished the beer at the feet of the deceased.
"We help both patients and their loved ones," says Nathalie Savard, director of care.
At Victor-Gadbois Centre, days pass without ever being the same.

Next to a 94-year-old man who is savoring his last family gathering in the yard, comfortably placed among his pillows while everyone drinks to his health, a 36-year-old man tragically dies, surrounded by his parents, his wife, and his two children, after having tried everything to survive
"For six months, there have always been three to five beds occupied by people under 45 years old suffering from cancer," worries Dr. Christiane Martel.
53% of the patients admitted to the Victor-Gadbois Center come from their home and 47% from the hospital.
Access to palliative care problem

A 77% of Canadians simply have no access to palliative care, that is, to care designed to relieve suffering when a patient reaches the terminal stage of their life, whether at home, in a hospital, or in a care facility.
And several organizations, such as the Victor-Gadbois Centre and the Home Palliative Care Society of Grand Montréal, specialize almost exclusively in the care of cancer patients.
It is precisely that great relative lack of healthcare in Quebec that makes many doctors specializing in palliative care fear the adoption of a law regulating euthanasia and assisted suicide.
Since October, a manifesto signed by prominent figures in palliative care, such as Dr. Balfour Mount and Dr. Bernard Lapointe, is circulating to demonstrate their opposition to such an initiative.
According to Dr. Christiane Martel, the healthcare system in Quebec is not competent enough to ensure that anyone has the right to quality palliative care before proceeding with euthanasia.
"Recently," she says, "I've seen a patient spend 14 days in the Emergency Department suffering great pain without anything being done to relieve her."
"I fear that patients may wish to die simply because they are not receiving adequate care."
And in parallel, many oncologists persist with their patients until the last day, despite the worst prognoses.
Hélène Richard's chances of survival were already at a low when she left an exhausting chemotherapy treatment.
"When I told my oncologist that I wanted to stop treatment, she said she was very sorry that I wanted to stop fighting," he reports.

Palliative care. The best way to die... | Le Devoir
In its Commission on Dying with Dignity, Quebec recently debated the delicate issue of end-of-life.
The debate must be resumed soon as a bill is being prepared.
Now, within that essential domain, there is still much to be done.
Le Devoir has tried to get close to him.
Just a few weeks ago, Mr. L. was living alone in his apartment in Montérégie.
The prostate cancer that was destroying him had given him a two-year reprieve.
"I had been given five years of life, but I've already lived seven," he recounts, a frail man lying in bed at the Victor-Gadbois palliative care center in Beloeil, where he arrived the day before.
"But it's always a shock, we can't be prepared for this," he continues.
The illness has caused him great trouble: a huge weakness that prevents him from going to the bathroom alone and even from eating by himself.
Sitting in front of a tempting lunch, he accepts resignedly that they help him eat.
Brave, he even smiles, talks to strangers who pay attention to him, bring him medicine, and offer him a bath.
The bravery of ordinary death.
"My greatest wish is that they cure my diarrhea, it's humiliating," he confesses.
A few hours later, the team found a remedy for that illness.
"Throughout our lives we learn that a man urinates standing up," says Pierre Brodeur, a psychologist at the Victor-Gadbois Centre.
Returning to one's childhood, for certain people, is an unacceptable humiliation.
"That depends on the person's ability to accept that regression," he notes.
Because, according to the opinion of most people who work in palliative care, the big moments take place in the very heart of that regression.
All patients who enter the Victor-Gadbois Palliative Care Centre suffer from cancer.
They have a maximum life expectancy of three months.
In that state, the team of doctors and nurses who surround them no longer offer "curative" care.
The greatest fear of Mrs. A., 89 years old, is to die "conscious and drowned".
But the illness has made him discover his children.
"I have some good children," he adds.
"I have no more wishes in this life," she says, before accepting that a mask will be placed on her to help her breathe.
And he is expecting, in the coming days, a final visit from his son who lives in Italy.
In Victor-Gadbois, with a group of volunteers, care of the body and help with feeding is offered.
They are palliative care that is given when nothing else can be done.
To help make his death more comfortable.
In Quebec, we have a palliative care bed for every 11,700 residents.
It's very little, since we know that we will all eventually die one day.
Here, life continues under the best possible conditions, explains Dr. Christiane Martel, one of the doctors at the center.
Whether in terms of physical comfort, emotional or spiritual well-being.
The dying man is given mouth washings with brandy or Pepsi, according to demand.
Diabetics are no longer monitored for their blood sugar levels.
Death is part of the everyday.
Last night we served a beer to Mr. X, who died during the night.
This morning, his son finished the beer at the feet of the deceased.
"We help both the patients and their loved ones," says Nathalie Savard, director of care.
At the Victor-Gadbois Centre, days pass without ever being the same.

Next to a 94-year-old man who is savoring his last family gathering in the yard, comfortably placed between his pillows while everyone drinks to his health, a 36-year-old man tragically dies, surrounded by his parents, his wife, and his two children, after having tried everything to survive
"For the past six months, there have always been three to five beds occupied by people under 45 with cancer," worries Dr. Christiane Martel.
53% of the patients admitted to the Victor-Gadboisarrivent center come from their home and 47% from the hospital.
Access to palliative care problem

77% of Canadians simply have no access to palliative care, that is, to care designed to relieve suffering when a patient reaches the terminal phase of their life, whether at home, in a hospital, or in a care facility.
And several organizations, such as the Victor-Gadbois Centre and the Home Palliative Care Society of Grand Montréal, specialize almost exclusively in the care of cancer patients.
It is precisely that great relative lack of healthcare in Quebec that makes many doctors specializing in palliative care fear the adoption of a law regulating euthanasia and assisted suicide.

Since October, a manifesto signed by prominent figures in palliative care, such as Dr. Balfour Mount and Dr. Bernard Lapointe, has been circulating to demonstrate their opposition to such an initiative.

According to Dr. Christiane Martel, the healthcare system in Quebec is not competent enough to ensure that anyone has the right to quality palliative care before proceeding with euthanasia is accepted.
"Recently," she says, "I have seen a patient spend 14 days in the Emergency Department suffering severe pain without anything being done to relieve her."
"I fear that patients want to die only because they are not receiving adequate care."
And in parallel, many oncologists persist with their patients until the last day, despite the worst prognoses.
Hélène Richard's chances of survival were already at a low when she left an exhausting chemotherapy treatment.
"When I told my oncologist that I wanted to stop treatment, she said she was very sorry that I wanted to stop fighting," he reports.
A Republican strategy to block Obama's re-election
Republican leaders justified their policy by the need to combat electoral fraud.
Now, the Brennan Center considers this last point a myth and claims that election fraud is less common in the United States than the number of people who die as a result of lightning strikes.
In fact, Republican lawyers have found no more than 300 cases of election fraud in the United States in ten years.
One thing is certain: these new provisions will negatively affect the voter turnout rate.
In that sense, these measures will undermine part of the American democratic system.
Unlike Canada, the American states are responsible for organizing federal elections in the United States.
And along those lines, a majority of American governments enacted, starting in 2009, new laws that made the registration or voting process more difficult.
This phenomenon has spread after the November 2010 elections, which saw the addition of 675 new Republican representatives in 26 states.
Consequently, during the year 2011, 180 bills were introduced that restricted the exercise of the right to vote in 41 states.
The new electoral laws require voters to present an ID with a photograph, as well as proof of American citizenship.

On the other hand, these laws reduce the periods for early voting, invalidate the right to register as a voter on the day of the election, and remove the right to vote from citizens with criminal records.
Before the 2006 elections, no American state required voters to present an ID with a photograph.
The State of Indiana was the first to demand it.
The U.S. Supreme Court confirmed in 2008 the constitutionality of the Indiana law.
Therefore, the Republican authorities hastened to extend that practice to other states.
In recent years, these authorities have supported 34 state bills to force voters to present a photo ID.
It is important to note that, unlike the situation in Quebec, American citizens do not have a universal identification document, such as the Social Security card.
In fact, 11% of American citizens, that is, 21 million voters, do not have any government-issued photo ID from their state's agency.
On the other hand, five million new voters in 2012 lack an ID document with those characteristics.
But often, obtaining the required ID document costs more than a hundred dollars.
Thus, the new restrictions disproportionately affect young people, minorities, and low-income individuals.
Indeed, 25% of African Americans, 15% of people earning less than $35,000 a year, 18% of citizens over 65 years old, and 20% of voters aged 18 to 29 do not have a photo ID.
And there's more.
In many states, students, the voters who most vote for Democratic candidates, cannot use the photo ID card issued by their institution.
On the other hand, those same states authorize members of hunting or fishing clubs, who usually vote for Republican parties, to use the documents issued by said clubs.
Before 2004, no state required a citizenship test to vote.
Arizona was the first state to make such a demand.
Since 2011, a dozen states have enacted laws requiring voters to demonstrate that they are American citizens.
Those measures clearly aim to limit the Hispanic vote.
It seems that two out of every three Hispanic voters support the Democratic Party.
On the other hand, Republican legislators supported in 2011 certain laws that eliminated same-day voter registration in eight states.
In addition, they limited the right of individuals and groups to create a voter assistance service for those who wanted to register.
These restrictions have consequences.
For example, in the 2004 general elections, voter registration campaigns contributed to the registration of about 10 million citizens.
The measures taken since 2009 caused the registration rate of new voters to fall in 2010 compared to the year 2006.
In addition, Republican legislators passed laws in five other states that favored the reduction of the early voting period.
For example, in the 2008 elections in Florida, 33% of the voters who voted early were African American, while these voters represented only 13% of the state's electorate.
In the case of Hispanics, exactly the same thing happened.
These represent no more than 11% of the voters, which is equivalent to 24% of the citizens who vote by advance voting.
However, the whites, who represent 76% of the electorate, represent only 46% of the citizens who vote in advance.
Of course, Democratic legislators and their supporters have strongly opposed the adoption of laws that restrict voter registration.
In this regard, Democratic governors have blocked several bills.
The U.S. Attorney General's Office intervened to suspend the most controversial laws.
The damage could, in part, be limited.
For example, only 16 of 34 states adopted the law requiring the presentation of an identity document with a photograph.
However, it is undeniable that the new rules adopted will complicate the exercise of the right to vote in 2012.
Democratic critics are denouncing the partisan nature of the laws that have been voted on, as it is clear that with them they intend to influence the results of 2012 in the key states.
A 2011 Brennan Center report shows that states that have adopted these laws account for 171 of the 270 electoral college votes needed to win the presidency.
It is too early to say with certainty whether these legislative changes at the electoral system level will have a significant impact on the results of the 2012 presidential elections.
One thing is certain: these new provisions will negatively affect the voter turnout rate.
In this regard, the measures will undermine part of the American democratic system.
Prostate Cancer Detection: To get tested or not to get tested?
Indeed, the PSA test sometimes produces erroneous results, with false negatives or even false positives, leading to unnecessary medical interventions.
It is more than sufficient reason for men, already reluctant by nature, to doubt whether they should undergo the detection tests.
To get tested or not?
We have consulted two specialists.
In studies conducted in the United States, a high rate of infection was detected among sample groups, making it difficult to interpret those data and make firm recommendations.
On the other hand, the European study showed some difference in mortality rates between patients who had undergone screening and those who had not.
The study, with a 12-year follow-up, also showed that there is between a 30 and 40% chance of developing metastases if the detection test has not been done.
I therefore recommend the test from the age of 50, or from the age of 40 if your father has had prostate cancer.
Black men have a higher risk index.
The key is to make a good decision once cancer is detected.
There are aggressive cancers and other cancers that are indolent.

It is truly necessary to ensure that the patient understands the degree of risk of his cancer. All possible options should be offered to him, and it is not necessarily required to treat prostate cancers that do not pose a long-term threat to life, in which case active disease monitoring should be preferred instead.
Today, many men who have been diagnosed with cancer are not treated, since the cancer is not aggressive and does not pose a risk to their lives.
Instead, we suggest active monitoring of the disease and, if it progresses, we offer them treatment.
We are increasingly determining precise criteria to decide who should or should not be treated.
I recommend that the test be done in any case.
But it is important that you speak with your doctor to determine whether you should take the test or not.
Movember, in collaboration with the International Society of Urology, has created a tool that allows evaluating the pros and cons of the PSA test.
This document can be downloaded (for now only in English, but translations will be available shortly) at the following link: http://ca.movember.com/fr/mens-health/prostate-cancer-screening
Prevent the disease
Unfortunately, there is no miracle cure to prevent cancer.
Despite the progress in research, the adoption of healthy lifestyle habits remains the best way to reduce the risk of suffering from the disease.
We estimate that if everyone ate well and moved enough, 30% of cancers could be prevented.
"If no one smoked, that rate would rise by at least 50%," emphasizes André Beaulieu, spokesperson for the Canadian Cancer Society.
In contrast, we estimate that about 10% of cancers are hereditary.
Many others remain totally inexplicable.
For the Canadian Cancer Society, the fight against smoking remains a priority despite the decrease in the number of smokers.
Tobacco is linked to 85% of lung cancer cases.
It also constitutes a risk factor for other types of cancer.
It seriously harms people's health.
"At present, there are still 1.5 million smokers in Quebec," said spokesperson André Beaulieu.
A hopeful fact: 10 years after quitting smoking, the risk of dying from cancer is reduced by half.
The peso
According to the SCC, fatness and obesity also contribute to the development of the disease.
They increase the risks of breast cancer, colon and rectal cancer, esophageal cancer, pancreatic cancer, and uterine cancer.
"Studies show that regular physical activity throughout life protects against breast cancer," they add.
The food
The body also recommends limiting the consumption of red meats.
In large amounts, they increase the risk of developing colorectal cancer.
Meat products should also be avoided.
The preservation of meat for smoking, drying, or salting may lead to the formation of carcinogenic substances.
"They can damage the body's cells and lead to the development of cancer," they explain to us.
The vitamins
In recent years, several scientists have studied the links between the complex vitamins and cancer.
However, at the moment their investigations are not conclusive.
According to the SCC, studies on vitamin E are contradictory.
While in one of them a decrease in the risk of prostate cancer was observed, in the other, what was observed was rather an increase.
The effect of vitamin D on cancer has not been clearly determined.
On the other hand, M. Beaulieu insists on the importance of discussing one's concerns and family history with their doctor.
"Taking the detection test does not cause cancer."
